text: What is the primary goal of Continuous Integration (CI)?
options: To automatically deploy every change straight to production
To frequently merge code changes into a shared branch and verify them with automated builds and tests
To replace manual code review entirely
To manage infrastructure provisioning across cloud providers
explanation: CI is the practice of merging developers' changes into a shared branch frequently, with each merge automatically built and tested to catch integration issues early.

text: What distinguishes Continuous Delivery from Continuous Deployment?
options: Continuous Delivery requires no automated testing, while Continuous Deployment does
There is no meaningful difference; the terms are interchangeable
Continuous Delivery ensures every change is release-ready but requires a manual approval to release, while Continuous Deployment releases automatically to production without manual intervention
Continuous Deployment only applies to mobile applications
explanation: Continuous Delivery keeps every build in a deployable state, with a human deciding when to release. Continuous Deployment goes one step further and automatically releases every passing build to production.

text: In trunk-based development, how do developers typically manage feature work that isn't ready for release?
options: They maintain long-lived feature branches for months until the feature is complete
They commit small, frequent changes directly to the trunk/main branch, often hidden behind feature flags
They fork the entire repository for each feature
They pause all other development until the feature ships
explanation: Trunk-based development favors short-lived branches or direct commits to main, using feature flags to hide incomplete work rather than isolating it in long-lived branches.

text: In Gitflow, which branch is typically used to prepare a new production release, allowing final bug fixes and version bumps?
options: hotfix
develop
release
feature
explanation: Gitflow's release branches are cut from develop to stabilize a version — final fixes and metadata updates happen here before merging into main and back into develop.

text: What is a key benefit of using feature flags in a delivery pipeline?
options: They eliminate the need for automated testing
They allow teams to merge and deploy incomplete or experimental code paths while keeping them disabled for users until ready
They automatically roll back failed deployments without configuration
They replace the need for a version control system
explanation: Feature flags decouple deployment from release, letting code ship to production dark (disabled) and be toggled on later, independent of the deploy process.

text: Which sequence best represents the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline?
options: Deploy → Build → Test → Monitor
Build → Test → Deploy → Monitor
Test → Deploy → Build → Monitor
Monitor → Build → Deploy → Test
explanation: A standard pipeline compiles/packages the code (build), validates it (test), releases it to an environment (deploy), and then observes it in production (monitor).

text: Why is it best practice to fail a pipeline fast when the build stage fails?
options: To give faster feedback to developers so they can fix issues before wasting time on later stages like testing and deployment
Because later pipeline stages are always more expensive to run financially
To avoid triggering notifications to the team
Failing fast has no real benefit, it's just a convention
explanation: Fail-fast pipelines surface problems as early as possible, minimizing wasted compute and giving developers rapid feedback instead of discovering build issues only after tests or deployment run.

text: What is the main difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
options: An image is a running instance of a container
A container is a running instance of an image; the image is the immutable template
Images and containers are the same thing with different names
A container can only run one image at a time forever, while images can run many containers
explanation: A Docker image is a read-only template containing the application and its dependencies. A container is a running (or stopped) instance created from that image.

text: What is the purpose of a Dockerfile?
options: It stores runtime logs generated by a container
It is a declarative set of instructions used to build a Docker image
It is a network configuration file for container orchestration
It replaces the need for a container registry
explanation: A Dockerfile contains step-by-step instructions (base image, copy files, install dependencies, set entrypoint, etc.) that Docker uses to build an image.

text: Why does Docker's layered filesystem matter for build performance?
options: It doesn't affect performance at all, layers are purely cosmetic
Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a cacheable layer, so unchanged layers can be reused, speeding up rebuilds
Layers must always be rebuilt from scratch on every build, regardless of caching
Layers only apply to Windows containers, not Linux containers
explanation: Docker caches each layer produced by a Dockerfile instruction. If an earlier layer hasn't changed, Docker reuses the cache instead of rebuilding it, significantly speeding up iterative builds.

text: Which of these is a defining characteristic of GitHub Actions compared to a traditional standalone CI server like Jenkins?
options: GitHub Actions workflows are defined in YAML files stored in the repository itself and are triggered natively by GitHub events
GitHub Actions requires a separately hosted master server that must be manually maintained by the team
GitHub Actions cannot run tests, only deployments
Jenkins is a cloud-only SaaS product with no self-hosting option
explanation: GitHub Actions workflows live as YAML in `.github/workflows/` and react directly to repository events (push, PR, release), whereas Jenkins traditionally runs as a separately maintained server with pipelines often defined via a Jenkinsfile or UI configuration.

text: In GitLab CI, what is the role of the `.gitlab-ci.yml` file?
options: It stores the project's README documentation
It defines the stages, jobs, and rules that make up the CI/CD pipeline for the repository
It is used exclusively for managing user permissions
It configures the Git commit message template
explanation: `.gitlab-ci.yml` is GitLab's pipeline configuration file, defining stages (e.g., build, test, deploy) and the jobs that run within them.

text: What is a blue-green deployment strategy?
options: Running two identical production environments where traffic is switched from the old (blue) to the new (green) version, enabling instant rollback
Gradually shifting a small percentage of traffic to a new version over time
Deploying updates to servers one at a time in a rolling sequence
A strategy that only applies to database schema migrations
explanation: Blue-green deployment maintains two full environments. Traffic is cut over to the new (green) environment once verified, and rollback is as simple as routing back to blue.

text: How does a canary deployment differ from a rolling deployment?
options: They are identical strategies with different names

A canary release exposes a new version to a small subset of users/traffic first to validate it before a full rollout, while a rolling deployment incrementally replaces all instances of the old version with the new one
A canary deployment requires downtime, while a rolling deployment never does
Rolling deployments are only used for database changes
explanation: Canary deployments limit exposure to a small slice of traffic to validate the new version's behavior in production before a broader rollout, while rolling deployments progressively update instances across the full fleet.

text: What core principle does Infrastructure as Code (IaC) rely on?
options: Manually configuring servers through a GUI to avoid documentation drift
Defining and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files that can be versioned, reviewed, and reused
Storing infrastructure credentials directly inside application source code
Avoiding automation to keep infrastructure changes auditable
explanation: IaC treats infrastructure configuration as code — version-controlled, reviewable, and repeatable — instead of manual, undocumented changes made through consoles or ad hoc scripts.

text: Why is idempotency an important property for Infrastructure as Code tools like Terraform?
options: It ensures running the same configuration multiple times produces the same end state without unintended side effects
It guarantees the infrastructure will never need to change again
It means the tool automatically writes application code for you
It has no practical importance in IaC tooling
explanation: Idempotent IaC tooling means applying the same configuration repeatedly converges to the same infrastructure state, making it safe to re-run without introducing drift or duplicate resources.

text: What is the primary difference between monitoring and observability?
options: Monitoring tracks predefined metrics and alerts against known failure modes, while observability provides the tools to explore and understand unknown or unanticipated system states
They are the exact same concept with different marketing names
Observability only refers to log storage, nothing else
Monitoring requires no dashboards or alerting
explanation: Monitoring answers 'is something wrong?' using known metrics and thresholds, while observability (via logs, metrics, and traces) lets engineers investigate novel or unexpected problems they didn't anticipate in advance.

text: Which three data types are commonly described as the 'three pillars of observability'?
options: Metrics, logs, and traces
Backups, snapshots, and archives
Commits, branches, and tags
Containers, images, and volumes
explanation: Metrics (numeric time-series data), logs (discrete event records), and traces (request flow across services) together give teams visibility into system behavior.

text: What does 'shift-left testing' mean in a DevOps context?
options: Moving testing activities earlier in the development lifecycle so defects are found and fixed sooner, rather than only at the end
Testing only after the application has been deployed to production
Reassigning all testing responsibilities exclusively to a dedicated QA team late in the cycle
Removing automated tests in favor of manual exploratory testing
explanation: Shift-left testing moves quality checks (unit tests, static analysis, security scans) earlier in the pipeline, closer to when code is written, reducing the cost and delay of fixing defects found later.

text: What is the purpose of an artifact repository (such as Nexus, Artifactory, or a container registry) in a CI/CD pipeline?
options: It stores and versions build outputs (binaries, packages, container images) so they can be reliably retrieved and deployed across environments
It is only used for storing source code, replacing the need for Git
It exists solely to host documentation for the project
It manages user authentication for the CI server
explanation: Artifact repositories store the versioned, immutable outputs of a build (JARs, npm packages, Docker images, etc.), ensuring the exact same artifact tested in CI is the one promoted through each environment to production.
